hints: Focus on separating the two jobs, count neutrons from mass number minus proton number, and count electrons from proton number adjusted for charge.
Work out your targets first, $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$ has 8 neutrons and $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}^{+}$ has 10 electrons.
Now test each option for both counts together, remembering that a negative charge means extra electrons, and pick the one that gives 8 neutrons and 10 electrons.
walkthrough:
**Find the number of neutrons to match**

Hi there, let us start with $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$. Neutrons are what is left after you take protons away from the mass.

$$\text{neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{proton number} = 14 - 6 = 8$$

**Find the number of electrons to match**

Now look at $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}^{+}$. A neutral Na atom has 11 electrons, but the 1+ charge means it has lost one electron.

$$\text{electrons} = 11 - 1 = 10$$

**Test each species for both numbers**

We need 8 neutrons and 10 electrons. For ions, remember to add electrons for negative charge.

$$\text{for }^{16}_{8}\text{O}^{2-}: \text{neutrons} = 16-8 = 8, \text{ electrons} = 8+2 = 10$$
This matches both targets perfectly, so this is our species.

options.A: Neutrons = 17 - 9 = 8 which is correct, but electrons = 9 because it is a neutral atom. It is one electron short of the 10 needed, so it only meets half the condition.
options.B: Electrons = 7 + 3 = 10 which is correct for the 3- ion, but neutrons = 16 - 7 = 9. It has one neutron too many, so it fails the neutron condition.
options.C: Electrons = 10 which is correct, but neutrons = 20 - 10 = 10. This is a common trap because it is isoelectronic with $\text{Na}^{+}$, but it does not have the same neutron count.
options.D: Neutrons = 16 - 8 = 8 and electrons = 8 + 2 = 10 for the 2- ion. It matches both the 8 neutrons of $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$ and the 10 electrons of $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}^{+}$, so it is correct.
